# Steering for the plain J-lens

I'd like a generic steering intervention that makes the plain J-lens read association's targets better. Add a vector
to Qwen3.5-4B's residual stream at some layers during the forward pass; the metric server then reads with the plain
(uncentred) J-lens at layers 26, 28 and 30 and scores strict pass@10 on association's `fit` split (102 items;
baseline 0.1275). `tools/metric.py` does all of that (`info`, `run`, `capture`; see CLAUDE.md); run
`.venv/bin/python tools/metric.py info` first.

Ground rules:

- The readout stays the plain J-lens. Only the forward pass changes.
- Steering vectors only: one vector per layer, added at the positions you choose (`prefix`, `read` or `context`).
- Directions, not means: each vector has to come from a contrast between two conditions (prompts or items you
  choose). Subtracting a mean, a prior or any other centring term is out of scope, at any layer or position.
- Generic: one intervention for every item, built without the targets. Nothing built from or optimised against the
  target words or the items' answers. Contrasts over prompts you write yourself are fine, as are captures of other
  families' items through `capture`.
- `fit` is all you see. A held-out split is scored separately and is not shown.
- The metric server is the only compute: no pods, no HF dataset, no `board.py`.
- It should be a new method, not a reproduction of an existing one.

There's some reading in `papers/` if it helps.

What I'd like back, in `submission/`:

1. `vectors.pt`: a dict `{layer: tensor[2560]}`, for `tools/metric.py run --positions prefix --scale 1.0`.
2. `contribution.md` (a paragraph or two): what the method is and where it came from.

I'll try the vectors when I'm back. What I'm looking for is novelty: an automated judge (an LLM I use
for this) reads contribution.md and scores it mainly on how new the method is, and it needs to reach about 0.50 on
fit to be worth using.

# What we already know about mu_l (imported 2026-10-10)

Synthesis of the centring work imported from `unverbalized-motivations` (now `umot/`,
source commit `30bbabf`) and `jlens-edits-1` (now `jle/`, source commit `5f483de`).
The records of truth are umot's `notes/research-log.md` and jle's `notes/predictions.md` (both upstream: unverbalized-motivations, jlens-edits-1);
this page only points into them.

## Setup shared by both lineages

- Lenses are the released ones, never refit: Qwen3.6-27B `neuronpedia/jacobian-lens …_n1000.pt`
  (wikitext, n=1000); `jle` also uses Qwen3.5-4B (neuronpedia, n=417) and Qwen3.5-9B instruct
  (`camilablank/workspace-lenses`, pile-10k). J_l = mean Jacobian of the final residual
  w.r.t. the block-l output. All in the HF cache, not in this repo.
- The released lens has **no mu**: it reads `J_l h`, an expansion around h = 0, which is off the data.
  Argument (umot log, 2026-10-09): `J(h - mu) ~ f(h) - f(mu)` is the coherent first-order readout;
  it justifies centring but does not pick mu. "Choosing mu is choosing the counterfactual."
  Framing on the umot dashboard: mu = E[h | C], a ladder of conditioning sets C.
- Two readouts, both linear in h, so a centred read is `L(h) - L(mu)`:
  `cos` (WorkspaceBench's): `(W_U J h)_t / ||J^T W_U[t]||`;
  `rms` (jle's): `rms_norm(J h, 1+w) W_U^T`. They disagree by up to 0.09 uncentred and
  agree within 0.033 after centring (x100). This is the README's "with/without norm" control.
- What centring removes: the mean decodes to the continuation prior (`<|im_end|>`, `\n\n`, This, The),
  ||mu|| / ||h|| = 0.81-0.98, and subtracting it removes 41-69 % of the norm (x98).

## The mu ladder so far

| mu | where | result |
|---|---|---|
| 0 (plain) | both | bench strict rate 0.55-0.68 pooled; DM judged content_bound 0.21 |
| mu_fit: the lens's own fit-corpus mean (`umot/out/fitmean/mu.pt`) | umot `fit_mean.py`, `fitmean_lin.py` | far better expansion point (held-out R² at L42 −0.13 → 0.15; OLS 0.47), but no better as a readout centre than the family mean; hurts on J++ evals (cos 0.357 → 0.313) |
| Taylor offsets `W_U(beta c + J(h - mu))` | umot `taylor_screen.py` | null: the mean Jacobian explains about 4 % of the variation at the read layers |
| generic corpus mean G1 (wikitext / pile) | jle x101 | does nothing |
| same-token corpus mean G2 | jle x101 | pooled +0.01 to +0.06; a quarter to a half of association's gain; harms 4 families somewhere |
| other families' mean (ctr1, x89d leave-one-family-out) | jle x89d, x99 | +0.02 to +0.08 |
| **own-family mean** (own1 / dev1 / loo / fam) | jle x97-x100, umot | bench, held out: rms 0.55/0.58/0.59 → 0.67/0.68/0.77 (4B/9B/27B); typo 27B 0.55 → 0.91; bootstrap SD < 0.01, 8 prompts suffice; multilingual −0.04 to −0.08 at 4B/9B, multihop mixed |
| own mean with top-k PCs removed (pco4/16), kNN, whitening | jle x90f-o, x96-x99 | +0.04 to +0.16 extra on multihop and 27B association; the mean is 88-100 % of pco4's gain |
| same read-token mean (tok1 / ctr-tok) | jle x99, umot | best on user_modeling; DM judged 0.21 → 0.82 |
| same sentence, same position (carpos) | umot | DM 0.89, **but reads the prompt**: see the mention control row |
| mention control (fairness test) | umot `mc_screen.py`, `validation_centring` | position-matched centres score held = mentioned (0.50/0.50); they separate only at sentence-final "." cells at L >= 42 (0.40 vs 0.15; rank 28 vs 1,834) |
| J++ lens (different map, not a centre) | umot `jpp_compare.py` | centring recovers about 45 % of the J-lens → J++ gap; centring J++ hurts it |
| J++ lens on our 11 families (`jpp:` arms) | `notes/jpp-compare.md` | plain J++ beats every J-lens arm on typo (bench 0.94 vs 0.76) and is at or above the plain J-lens on the single-token families; centring J++ is mixed (helps association, hurts basic_readout / multilingual); not judged yet |

### Added by the constant-μ section (x1-x25, closed 2026-10-12; `notes/constant-mu.md`, "Conclusions")

Dev val, strict, rms, pooled over the five plain families, vs the plain J-lens.

| mu | where | result |
|---|---|---|
| mean final-token state of ~64 short texts the model writes, no task named (`glos:none`) | x14 B, x24 | data-free; +0.176 (family mean +0.216); naming the task (glossary word) adds ~0.02; needs the sentence-end read (one word earlier: +0.010); wikitext sentences +0.015 to +0.046 |
| per-input situation / topic word | x23, x23b | below a constant: +0.115 to +0.130 / −0.109 |
| J++ + data-free centre | x19b, x25 | +0.00 to +0.03 over J++ pooled (+0.10 on association); bench: J++ + glossary word 0.854, the best data-free arm |

## Lessons

1. The gain comes from a **matched counterfactual**, not from a better expansion point
   (mu_fit linearises better and still doesn't help as a readout).
2. One mu per layer only adds a fixed token bias. It works on WorkspaceBench because every item
   reads the same template cell, so the family mean is effectively position- and token-matched.
   On DM, read cells vary, so the family mean does nothing and a token- or position-matched mu is needed.
3. Tighter matching removes more noise but also more content: it starts reading or subtracting
   the prompt. This is the README's "fair / not cheating" axis. x101: the reference must match the
   read cell's form and context, not just its token. **The open problem is a label-free,
   context-matched mu.**

## README ideas vs prior work

- Partly done: norm vs no norm (the two readouts); position (carpos); token (tok1, G2);
  clusters (kNN ≈ pco); n-scaling (8 / 32 / all reference prompts, flat beyond 8);
  dynamic g(h_t, h_{t-1}, …), which is only listed, not run (umot `dashboard/views/centring_story.py` §7:
  self-truncation, corpus conditional mean g(token, last k), kNN retrieval, prediction deflation).
- Not done: a random-vector mu as a control; an abstract-word or steering-vector mu;
  an "optimal" mu reconstructed from targets (under jle's "no crystal ball" rule this is an
  in-sample ceiling, not a method); further WorkspaceBench dev and validation sets beyond dev bank v2.

## Where things are

- umot: `src/umot/centring.py` (concept-aware `Centre`), `experiments/token_local.py`
  (every centred arm, runs on the Mac from captures), `out/captures/` (residuals at read cells),
  `out/fitmean/mu.pt`, `out/jpp/residuals.pt`, `dashboard/` (Streamlit; pages "Centring",
  "Centring: bench to wild", "Validation: centring", "J++ vs centring", "Token tracker").
- jle: `experiments/x95…x101_*.py` (they import x89 / x90 / x90c / x90f modules as libraries),
  `data/x90-dev/bank-v2` (dev bank), `out/x96-capture-*.pt` (association residuals at every
  position), `out/x101-means-*.pt` (corpus and per-token means), x95-x101 stores and reports,
  `out/x100-summary.md`, `lensboard/` (`#/centre` page; banks dev4 / dev5 / bench2).

1	"""Client for the steering metric server (the model runs on the GPU box; this machine only sends requests).
2	
3	The server holds Qwen3.5-4B and its J-lens, and scores a steering intervention on the association dev split:
4	strict pass@10 and the mean log10 best target rank, read with the plain J-lens at the layers after the band.
5	
6	    python tools/metric.py info
7	    python tools/metric.py run out/steer/v.pt [--positions prefix|read|context] [--scale 1.0]
8	    python tools/metric.py capture spec.json --out out/steer/means.pt
9	
10	``v.pt`` is ``{layer: tensor[d_model]}``: added to the residual stream at the output of each listed block. A capture
11	spec is JSON: ``{"layers": [...], "prompts": [{"user": ..., "assistant": ...}], "positions": "last" | "user" |
12	"assistant" | "all"}``, or ``{"layers": [...], "bench_items": [ids], "family": ..., "split": ...}`` to read a bench
13	bank's own read cells. The server address is ``JLM_METRIC_URL`` (default ``http://localhost:8765``).
14	"""
15	
16	import argparse
17	import base64
18	import json
19	import os
20	import sys
21	import urllib.request
22	
23	import torch
24	
25	URL = os.environ.get("JLM_METRIC_URL", "http://localhost:8765")
26	
27	
28	def _call(path: str, body: dict | None = None, timeout: float = 900) -> dict:
29	    data = None if body is None else json.dumps(body).encode()
30	    req = urllib.request.Request(URL + path, data=data, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
31	    try:
32	        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as r:
33	            return json.loads(r.read())
34	    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
35	        raise RuntimeError(json.loads(e.read()).get("error", str(e))) from None
36	
37	
38	def _enc(t: torch.Tensor) -> dict:
39	    return {"b64": base64.b64encode(t.detach().float().cpu().contiguous().numpy().tobytes()).decode()}
40	
41	
42	def _dec(x: dict) -> torch.Tensor:
43	    t = torch.frombuffer(bytearray(base64.b64decode(x["b64"])), dtype=torch.float32).clone()
44	    return t.reshape(x["shape"])
45	
46	
47	def info() -> dict:
48	    return _call("/info")
49	
50	
51	def run_metric(vectors: dict[int, torch.Tensor], positions: str = "prefix", scale: float = 1.0) -> dict:
52	    """Score ``vectors`` (layer -> [d_model]) added at ``positions`` of every item; returns the fit numbers."""
53	    return _call("/run_metric", {"vectors": {str(L): _enc(v) for L, v in vectors.items()}, "positions": positions,
54	                                 "scale": scale})
55	
56	
57	def capture(spec: dict) -> dict:
58	    """Residual means for a capture spec: ``{"n_prompts", "layers", "mean": {L: [d]}, "per_prompt"?: {L: [n, d]}}``."""
59	    out = _call("/capture", spec)
60	    for k in ("mean", "per_prompt"):
61	        if k in out:
62	            out[k] = {int(L): _dec(v) for L, v in out[k].items()}
63	    return out
64	
65	
66	def main() -> None:
67	    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
68	    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)
69	    sub.add_parser("info")
70	    r = sub.add_parser("run")
71	    r.add_argument("vectors")
72	    r.add_argument("--positions", default="prefix", choices=("prefix", "read", "context"))
73	    r.add_argument("--scale", type=float, default=1.0)
74	    c = sub.add_parser("capture")
75	    c.add_argument("spec")
76	    c.add_argument("--out", required=True)
77	    a = ap.parse_args()
78	    if a.cmd == "info":
79	        print(json.dumps(info(), indent=1))
80	    elif a.cmd == "run":
81	        vecs = {int(L): v for L, v in torch.load(a.vectors, weights_only=False).items()}
82	        print(json.dumps(run_metric(vecs, a.positions, a.scale), indent=1, ensure_ascii=False))
83	    else:
84	        with open(a.spec) as f:
85	            out = capture(json.load(f))
86	        torch.save(out, a.out)
87	        print(f"{out['n_prompts']} prompts, layers {out['layers']} -> {a.out}", file=sys.stderr)
88	
89	
90	if __name__ == "__main__":
91	    main()

# Shared workflow (for both collaborators and their agents)

Two people (Maya, Anthony) and their Claude instances work in this repo. This is how code, results and the
dashboard move between them. `CLAUDE.md` points every session here; read it before running experiments,
changing the pipeline or the dashboard, or pushing.

## Branches

| branch | holds | who changes it |
|---|---|---|
| `eval-pipeline` | shared infrastructure: the pipeline (`src/jlm`, `experiments/{evaluate,judge,analyse,report,agreement}.py`, capture), the data sync (`jlm.hfdata`, `tools/hfdata.py`), the dashboard framework and its generic pages and helpers, `tools/deploy_space.py`, these instructions | either, for things the other also needs; both merge it into their own branch |
| `constant-mean-exploration` | Maya's experiments (x1-x12, `src/jlm/mu/constant_mu.py`), their notes and dashboard page | Maya and her agents |
| `iteration` | Anthony's research loop (`src/jlm/mu/<study>.py`, `notes/iteration-anthony/`) and its pages | Anthony and his agents |

- Infrastructure goes to `eval-pipeline`: a pipeline fix, a new dashboard helper or generic page, sync or deploy
  changes. Keep it working (`.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests`) and never force-push it.
- Study content stays on its branch: centres in `src/jlm/mu/<study>.py`, study scripts, study notes, study pages,
  and their `dashboard/catalog.py` entries (names, colours, `OPT_IN` heads).
- Merge `origin/eval-pipeline` into your branch before running experiments, and run them from your branch's
  checkout: provenance stamps every artefact with branch@commit. In a git worktree run with
  `PYTHONPATH=src:umot/src` (the shared venv's `umot` points at the main checkout, and provenance stamps the
  checkout `umot` is imported from).
- Push a shared branch (`eval-pipeline`), or anyone else's, only when its owner says so.

## Results: the shared dataset

Everything under the git-ignored `out/` lives in one private HF dataset, `[org]/j-lens-mean-data`
(`notes/eval-pipeline.md`, "Shared data on Hugging Face").

- Every pipeline step pushes what it wrote as it finishes (`hfdata.share`): `evaluate.py` the bank's directory,
  `judge.py` the run's directory, `analyse.py` the study's directory, capture and the generators their capture.
  It needs a login with write access to the org (`hf auth login`, or `HF_TOKEN` on a pod); without one it says
  so and the run goes on. Push anything else with `python tools/hfdata.py push <subpaths>`.
- Throwaway runs: `JLM_HF_AUTOPUSH=0`, or write them outside `out/` (`--out /tmp/...`): neither is shared.
- `python tools/hfdata.py pull` brings the other side's results into your `out/`; it never overwrites a file
  you changed since your last sync, and bank summaries merge (both sides' arms kept).
- One arm name, one meaning: the same arm on the same bank from different code is a conflict in the dataset
  (listed by the push, not overwritten). Give a new variant a new centre name.

## The dashboard

One shared copy: https://huggingface.co/spaces/[org]/j-lens-mean-dashboard (private to the org; log in
to HF). It is `eval-pipeline` merged with the branches in `.github/dashboard-branches`, redeployed by
`.github/workflows/deploy-dashboard.yml` on every push to one of them that touches the dashboard or the code it
imports. Results appear without a deploy: the Space pulls the dataset every 5 minutes ("Shared data" page: what
arrived, from whom, from which branch).

- A page for your study: `dashboard/views/<page>.py` on your branch, listed in `dashboard/app.py`'s navigation.
  It reaches the shared dashboard on your next push. Use the helpers that exist on `eval-pipeline`
  (`sources`, `ui`, `catalog`, `figures`); a new helper, or a change to one, goes to `eval-pipeline` first.
- Two branches changing the same lines stop the deploy; the workflow's log names the files. Resolve it on one
  branch (usually: move the shared part to `eval-pipeline`) and push again.
- Locally: `.venv/bin/streamlit run dashboard/app.py` shows your branch with the same synced data.
- By hand (no CI): `python tools/deploy_space.py --space [org]/j-lens-mean-dashboard --dataset
  [org]/j-lens-mean-data` (merges the branches from origin; `--stage DIR` builds without uploading).

47	    if split not in SPLITS + HELD_OUT:

49	    return DEV_ROOT / family / f"{split}.json"

51

53	    path = path_of(family, split)

77	    if bank.split == "bench":

89	    orig = readplan._bank

92	        return (bank.header, bank.items) if family == bank.family else orig(family)

content.thinking:
Now I understand the association benchmark structure. It's a "guess the missing concept" task: the prompt describes a situation, and the model must output the concept word.

The readout reads a cell (probably the final token position of the prompt, i.e., the next-token prediction, using the J-lens to read the logits). Actually let me understand: the J-lens reads `J_l h_l` = final residual (logits) as a linear function of block-l output. So the readout predicts the logits of the next token from the current hidden state. The "plain J-lens" reads at layers 26, 28, 30, and scores "strict pass@10" — the target word must be within the top 10 predictions.

So the task is: the model reads the prompt, and the plain J-lens predicts the next token. We want the target word to appear in the top-10.

Now, the steering: add a vector v at some positions (prefix, read, context) to bias the model toward producing the correct next-token concept.

Constraint: Generic — one intervention for every item, built without targets. Nothing from target words. Contrasts over prompts we write ourselves or captures of other families' items.

Key idea candidates:
1. Contrast between "task-like" prompts that require identifying a concept vs. neutral prompts — steering toward "identify the concept" behavior. This is essentially the classic ActAdd: contrast between prompts that elicit a behavior and prompts that don't. E.g., "Identify the underlying concept:" vs generic text.

2. The plain J-lens reads uncentred `J_l h`. The "problem" is that mu is uncentred (mu=0). But we can't change the readout, only the forward pass. However, we CAN improve the readout by making h_l more "centred" relative to the lens's expansion point, i.e., make the final residual's logits-less component smaller... hmm.

Actually, let me think about what the J-lens readout actually computes and where the error comes from.

J_l = mean Jacobian ∂(final residual)/∂(block-l output). The readout approximates the final logits as J_l h_l (via the W_U projection). The error of this approximation is the second-order term. The plain readout is `(W_U J_l h_l)_t / norm`.

To make the lens read the target better, we can steer the hidden state so that the first-order term J_l h_l already points more at the target. But we can't use targets.

Alternative framing from the synthesis: The open problem is "label-free, context-matched mu". The steering version: instead of subtracting a mu from the readout, ADD a steering vector v to the forward pass such that the bias is baked in.

Actually, the task says "Directions, not means: each vector has to come from a contrast between two conditions". So the vector is a contrast direction (difference between two mean states).

Let me think about what contrast would generically improve a "concept completion" readout.

Idea A: Function/behavior vector for "name the unifying concept/category of this description". Contrast:
- "+" prompts: "What single word best describes the situation above?" / examples where the model is prompted to produce a category label.

"""The read plan: for every item of every family, what to feed the model, how to render it,
which token positions to read, and at which layers. `wsbench plan` writes it as JSONL; `resolve`
turns a positions rule into token indices once a producer has tokenized the render."""

import json
import re
from collections.abc import Iterable
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from wsbench.banks import load_bank as load_bank_file
from wsbench.registry import REPO_ROOT

GRID = list(range(20, 61, 4))  # the benchmark's layer grid for Qwen3.6-27B (64 layers)
SIX = [20, 28, 36, 44, 52, 60]  # the association families' coarser grid
FIVE = [20, 36, 44, 52, 60]  # the in-house layers of the hallucination and jailbreak arms
ANSWER_STEM = "My one-word answer is:"  # basic_readout implicit items: prefilled assistant turn
SUMMARIZE_SUFFIX = "\n\nSummarize the preceding story in one sentence."

RENDERS: dict[str, str] = {
    "plain": "the text verbatim, no chat template, no special tokens",
    "chat": "Qwen chat template, enable_thinking=False (empty <think> block); the text is the "
    "user turn, `system` the system turn when the item carries one; read positions index the "
    "full render",
    "chat_context": "Qwen chat template over the item's `messages` (system + user), "
    "enable_thinking=False; read positions index the full render",
    "chat_prefill": "Qwen chat template, enable_thinking=False; the text is the user turn and "
    "`prefill` is appended verbatim as the start of the assistant turn",
    "chat_dm": "Qwen chat template; the prompt is the user turn and `assistant` is the "
    "teacher-forced assistant turn (the carrier sentence the model copies)",
    "chat_summarize": "Qwen chat template, enable_thinking=False, no system prompt; the user turn "
    "is the stimulus followed by `suffix`",
    "bare": "the text verbatim with nothing asked (a program, a scene), no chat template",
    "captured": "the exact captured token ids (`input_ids`) shipped with the bank; positions "
    "index them directly",
}


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReadSpec:
    """One item's read plan. ``positions`` is a rule (see ``resolve``); ``layers`` the layers to
    read; ``text`` / ``messages`` / ``prefill`` / ``suffix`` what to render under ``render``."""

    family: str
    id: str
    render: str
    positions: dict[str, Any]
    layers: list[int]
    text: str | None = None
    messages: list[dict[str, str]] | None = None
    system: str | None = None
    prefill: str | None = None
    suffix: str | None = None
    assistant: str | None = None
    note: str = ""
    extra: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def row(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        d = asdict(self)
        return {k: v for k, v in d.items() if v not in (None, "", {}, [])}


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- positions rules
#
# kinds:
#   final_token                 the last token of the render
#   offset_from_end {k}         the token k from the end (k=1 is the last), reported as the
#                               negative index -k, the convention of the banks that use it
#   last_n {n}                  the last n tokens
#   all                         every token
#   all_from_end                every token, reported as negative offsets -n..-1 (the
#                               convention of the banks that count from the end)
#   positions {list}            explicit indices into the render
#   line_one_newline            the newline token that ends line one (the last newline)
#   from_token {token}          from the first token whose text is `token` through the end
#   from_last_sentence_start    from the first token of the final sentence of the last user
#                               turn through the end of the render
#   suffix_text {text}          the tokens whose joined text is `text` at the end of the render
#   suffix_text_then_tail       `suffix_text` plus every token after it (the chat tail)


def _clean(tok: str) -> str:
    return tok.replace("Ġ", " ").replace("▁", " ").replace("Ċ", "\n")


def resolve(rule: dict[str, Any], tokens: list[str]) -> list[int]:
    """Token indices a rule selects over ``tokens`` (the render's token strings, byte-level BPE
    display or plain). Every kind above is handled; unknown kinds raise."""
    n = len(tokens)
    kind = rule["kind"]
    if kind == "final_token":
        return [n - 1] if n else []
    if kind == "offset_from_end":
        k = int(rule["k"])
        return [-k] if 0 < k <= n else []
    if kind == "last_n":
        return list(range(max(0, n - int(rule["n"])), n))
    if kind == "all":
        return list(range(n))
    if kind == "all_from_end":
        return list(range(-n, 0))
    if kind == "positions":
        return [int(p) for p in rule["positions"] if 0 <= int(p) < n]
    if kind == "line_one_newline":
        nls = [i for i, t in enumerate(tokens) if "\n" in _clean(t)]
        return [nls[-1]] if nls else []
    if kind == "from_token":
        want = rule["token"]
        hits = [i for i, t in enumerate(tokens) if _clean(t) == want or t == want]
        return list(range(hits[0], n)) if hits else []
    if kind == "from_last_sentence_start":
        return _from_last_sentence_start(tokens)
    if kind in ("suffix_text", "suffix_text_then_tail"):
        start = _suffix_start(tokens, rule["text"])
        if start is None:
            return []
        if kind == "suffix_text_then_tail":
            return list(range(start, n))
        end = _text_end(tokens, start, rule["text"])
        return list(range(start, end))
    raise ValueError(f"unknown positions rule {kind!r}")


def _from_last_sentence_start(tokens: list[str]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(tokens)
    ends = [i for i, t in enumerate(tokens) if t == "<|im_end|>"]
    starts = [
        i
        for i, t in enumerate(tokens)
        if t == "<|im_start|>" and i + 1 < n and tokens[i + 1] == "user"
    ]
    if not starts or not ends:
        return list(range(n))
    u0 = starts[-1]
    u1 = next((e for e in ends if e > u0), n)
    body = list(range(u0 + 3, u1))  # skip <|im_start|>, user, newline
    if not body:
        return list(range(u1, n))
    i = body[-1] - 1
    while i > body[0]:
        if re.search(r"[.!?]\s*$", _clean(tokens[i])):
            break
        i -= 1
    start = i + 1 if i > body[0] else body[0]
    return list(range(start, n))


def _suffix_start(tokens: list[str], text: str) -> int | None:
    """Index where the joined token text last begins ``text`` (leading whitespace ignored)."""
    target = text.strip()
    for start in range(len(tokens) - 1, -1, -1):
        joined = "".join(_clean(t) for t in tokens[start:]).lstrip()
        if joined.startswith(target):
            return start
    return None


def _text_end(tokens: list[str], start: int, text: str) -> int:
    target = text.strip()
    acc = ""
    for i in range(start, len(tokens)):
        acc = (acc + _clean(tokens[i])).lstrip() if not acc else acc + _clean(tokens[i])
        if len(acc) >= len(target):
            return i + 1
    return len(tokens)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- per-family plans


def _bank(family: str) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], list[dict[str, Any]]]:
    path = REPO_ROOT / "evals" / family / "items.json"
    raw = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    if isinstance(raw, list):  # the plain-list banks already carry ids
        return {}, raw
    if raw["items"] and "name" not in raw["items"][0]:  # wrapped banks keyed on id
        return {k: v for k, v in raw.items() if k != "items"}, raw["items"]
    header, items = load_bank_file(path)
    return header, items


def _final_token_families(family: str, render: str) -> list[ReadSpec]:
    _h, items = _bank(family)
    out = []
    for it in items:
        rule = {"kind": "final_token"}
        spec = it.get("readout") or {}
        if spec.get("kind") in ("final_prompt_token", "last_word_token") and spec.get("offsets"):
            k = -int(spec["offsets"][0])
            rule = {"kind": "final_token"} if k == 1 else {"kind": "offset_from_end", "k": k}
        r = it.get("eval_render") or render
        if r == "chat":  # basic_readout's implicit items: the model's own favourite after the stem
            out.append(
                ReadSpec(
                    family,
                    it["id"],
                    "chat_prefill",
                    rule,
                    GRID,
                    text=it["prompt"],
                    prefill=ANSWER_STEM,
                )
            )
        else:
            out.append(ReadSpec(family, it["id"], r, rule, GRID, text=it["prompt"]))
    return out


def plan(family: str) -> list[ReadSpec]:
    """The read plan for one family, one ReadSpec per bank item."""
    if family in (
        "association",
        "basic_readout",
        "multihop",
        "multilingual",
        "typo",
        "basic_readout_mt",
        "multihop_mt",
        "multilingual_mt",
        "multilingual_multihop",
        "multilingual_typo",
        "typo_mt",
    ):
        return _final_token_families(family, "plain")
    if family == "poetry":
        _h, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "plain",
                {"kind": "line_one_newline"},
                GRID,
                text=it["prompt"],
                note="the newline that ends line one of the couplet",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "directed_modulation":
        _h, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "chat_dm",
                {"kind": "suffix_text", "text": it["assistant"]},
                GRID,
                text=it["prompt"],
                assistant=it["assistant"],
                note="every token of the teacher-forced carrier sentence",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "user_modeling":
        _h, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "chat_context",
                {"kind": "from_last_sentence_start"},
                GRID,
                messages=it["messages"],
                note="the request sentence through the end of the render, template tokens included",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "moral_rationale":
        _h, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "chat",
                {"kind": "last_n", "n": 5},
                GRID,
                text=it["stimulus"],
                note="the last five positions of the render",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "relational_multihop":
        _h, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "bare",
                {"kind": "final_token"},
                GRID,
                text=it["stimulus"],
                note="the possessive blank that ends the cloze",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family in ("conjunctive_association", "role_bound_association"):
        _h, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "chat_summarize",
                {"kind": "suffix_text_then_tail", "text": SUMMARIZE_SUFFIX.strip()},
                SIX,
                text=it["stimulus"],
                suffix=SUMMARIZE_SUFFIX,
                note="the 19 suffix and chat-tail tokens; story positions are never "
                "read (docs/read_sites.md)",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "brew_intermediates":
        _h, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "chat_prefill",
                {"kind": "positions", "positions": it["eval_positions"]},
                GRID,
                text=it["prompt"],
                prefill="Answer:",
                extra={"regions": it["regions"]},
                note="24 pinned cells: the three emission cells (the headline) plus the stir, "
                "start and question regions",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "chain_intermediates":
        _h, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "chat",
                {"kind": "from_token", "token": " What"},
                GRID,
                text=it["prompt"],
                note="the question span through the end of the render (opts=cells=all); the "
                "default judge reads only the render's final token, the assistant onset",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "arithmetic_intermediates":
        _h, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "chat",
                {"kind": "all_from_end"},
                [56, 60],
                text=it["prompt"],
                extra={"variant": it["variant"], "frozen_cell": it["cell"]},
                note="every position at layers 56 and 60 (opts=cells=all, the regime of record); "
                "frozen_cell is the pre-registered (layer, negative offset) the default judge "
                "reads",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "buggy_code":
        header, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "bare",
                {"kind": "final_token"},
                [int(header["read_cells"][it["lang_group"]]["layer"])],
                text=it["code"],
                note="the end of the file; layer 60 for python, 56 otherwise",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "multi_concept_directed_modulation":
        header, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "chat_prefill",
                {"kind": "last_n", "n": 12},
                [int(x) for x in header["layers"]],
                text=it["prompt"],
                prefill=header["target_sentence"],
                note="every token of the prefilled target sentence",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "hallucination":
        rows = json.loads((REPO_ROOT / "evals/hallucination/capture_rows.json").read_text())
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                r["id"],
                "captured",
                {"kind": "positions", "positions": r["read_positions"]},
                FIVE,
                extra={"input_ids": r["input_ids"], "prompt_len": r["prompt_len"]},
                note="punctuation and newline sites inside the model's own response, at the "
                "five in-house layers",
            )
            for r in rows
        ]
    if family == "jailbreak_recognition":
        from wsbench.evals.jailbreak_recognition.judge import grid_positions, prefix_to_last_user

        _h, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "chat_context",
                {"kind": "positions", "positions": grid_positions(it["read"])},
                FIVE,
                messages=prefix_to_last_user(it["messages"]),
                extra={"n_tokens": it["read"]["n_tokens"]},
                note="every token of the last user turn, first content token through its "
                "<|im_end|> (read.span); the bank's n_tokens also closes an empty assistant "
                "turn, two tokens past the generation prompt and past every read position",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "agentic_misalignment":
        _h, items = _bank(family)
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                it["id"],
                "chat",
                {"kind": "all"},
                [*GRID, 63],
                text=it["text"],
                system=it.get("system"),
                note="every prompt position of the chat render (system + user); the pinned "
                "rollout is not read",
            )
            for it in items
        ]
    if family == "jlens_concept_pr":
        m = json.loads((REPO_ROOT / "evals/jlens_concept_pr/manifest.json").read_text())
        return [
            ReadSpec(
                family,
                p["label"],
                "captured",
                {"kind": "positions", "positions": p["eval_positions"]},
                GRID,
                extra={"n_pos": p["n_pos"], "source_family": p["family"]},
                note="the text is not shipped; recapture from the source repo's items",
            )
            for p in m["prompts"]
        ]
    raise KeyError(f"no read plan for {family!r}")


def families() -> list[str]:
    return sorted(
        p.name
        for p in (REPO_ROOT / "evals").iterdir()
        if (p / "items.json").exists() or (p / "manifest.json").exists()
    )


def write(specs: Iterable[ReadSpec], path: Path) -> int:
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    n = 0
    with path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for s in specs:
            fh.write(json.dumps(s.row(), ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
            n += 1
    return n

234	together show is item-level, not categorical.

  something G2 cannot. The joint (token, position-bucket) mean G2xP is the finer rung but
  needs more reference tokens per cell (sparsity — watch n per bucket).
- **Implementation is small**: `x101_generic_mean.py`'s accumulator already holds
  `[n_layers, n_pos, d]` residuals per passage and keys float64 sums by token id; add a
  per-position (and per token x pos-bucket) sum alongside. `jle/out/` is not live, so the
  means must be regenerated anyway (pod for 27B; 4B/9B were jle's local models).

The decomposition in "Why this arm is worth running" then gains a term:

    mu_fam  ~=  token prior (G2)  +  position prior (P)  +  category direction (alpha*v)  +  residual

## First experiment sketch

Arms {0, G2, P, G2+P, v alone, G2+P + alpha*v (task word), G2+P + alpha*v (hypernym), fam} at 27B on
3-4 families spanning the table: **brew** (tight hypernym), **typo** (task=hypernym, big
fam gain 0.55->0.91), **association** (heterogeneous golds, biggest fam gain), **multihop**
(fam was mixed). Captures for the x89/x90 banks are archived on the desktop
(`jle/notes/archive-manifest/`); association residuals exist as `jle/out/x96-capture-*.pt`
per synthesis, but spills were not imported — check what is live before planning pod time.
Register predictions per `jle/notes/predictions.md` before judging. Headline read: how much
of (fam − G2) do P and alpha*v each recover on top of G2, per family.

Prediction to register (mine): v alone ~ null on bench template cells (lesson 2);
G2 + alpha*v recovers a visible minority of the fam gain on association and
conjunctive_association (semantically coherent categories), little on typo (its fam gain
looks like token-prior removal at a fixed cell), and the brew hypernym ladder shows
colour > property > concept.

## Where the global-workspace concept set stands after x1-x6 (2026-10-10)

As SUBTRACTION material the GW content types failed: per-sample dictionary words = the
derangement control pooled (x2, x3), and content-type words actively delete the signal where the
answer instantiates the type (user_modeling -0.39). What survives of the taxonomy:
(1) the frame / content split it made visible — the workspace's situational FRAME is subtractable
("typo": +0.09..+0.18 held out across x3/x5), its content type never is; (2) the model can NAME
the workspace content type per sample (the 27B self-labels, 85 % on typo) — a capability result
independent of mu; (3) as a diagnostic, the taxonomy predicts which reads a constant helps
(frame-salient, content-orthogonal cells) and which it harms. Untested GW material: the
self_meta group (secret / thought / reason / plan), which lives in DM, moral_rationale and
agentic_misalignment — the families where frames should be strongest ("I am holding a secret") —
plus group-level directions (one vector per GW type; x2's derangement result predicts null) and
frame PROPOSITIONS as carriers ("There is a typo in this sentence." as a state, not a word).
DM is the decisive next test: umot's tok1 took DM judged 0.21 -> 0.82, and a secret-frame mu
needs no token matching to try.

## x1 results (2026-10-10, typo only; registration and outcome in notes/predictions.md)

Both arms ran at 27B on typo fit/val (dev bank), strict free tier, captures and reads local
(3x A100 box). Val, n=91, vs zero 0.692/0.571 (cos/rms); fam@fit = 0.923/0.901.

- **Position: null.** pos@corpus -0.011 cos / -0.055 rms vs zero; fam@corpus8, tok@corpus8 and
  fam@sents the same or worse. On typo (reads at positions 5-11, where the early-position norm
  structure lives) a position-matched neutral-corpus mu removes nothing the readout cares
  about. The "position prior" term of the decomposition is ~0 here; P still untested where read
  cells vary (DM, user_modeling).
- **Abstract word: real but partial, and readout-dependent.** cpt:typo:1 beats the matched
  giraffe control by +0.194 cos [+0.097,+0.291] (also +0.097 at alpha 0.5), taking zero 0.69 ->
  0.78-0.80; under rms the concept-specific part is +0.043 [-0.054,+0.140] and the arm's gain
  is mostly the generic any-word norm effect (+0.077). "misspelling" carries about half the
  typo effect (+0.086 cos, CI includes 0); alpha = 2 harms; the carrier-free contrast direction
  (cptc) is null-to-harmful on its own.
- **The family mean stays 0.12-0.22 ahead** of the best abstract-word arm (paired, outside the
  bootstrap). With token, position, genericity and category semantics all now measured and
  insufficient, what remains of mu_fam's gain on typo is item-level family content at the read
  cell (correction-shaped / orthographic structure). That sharpens the open problem: the
  label-free mu must reconstruct that, not the category.

Revisits to the sketch above: the prediction "little on typo" was wrong in an interesting way —
the concept component is the one piece that does transfer under cos; the corpus rungs
(G1/G2/P/sentence-end), which x101 measured as small-positive pooled, are flat-to-negative on
typo val at 27B.

## Per-sample selection from a global dictionary (x2, 2026-10-10)

The dictionary (`data/abstract_concepts.json`, 30 words + 3 neutral) spans the six single-token
families' data: family words (typo/theme/answer/fact/meaning/identity), stratum words from bank
metadata (basic_readout subfamilies; user_modeling `attr_class`: country/continent/gender/
occupation/religion/diet/marriage/pet/job/age) and data-level hypernyms (month, element, organ,
number, game, place, organization, person, event, emotion, colour, word, language).

Label-free GEOMETRIC selection is weak on typo fit: argmax cosine of (h − sentence-end mean)
against neutral-contrast carrier directions picks "typo" for 22 % of cells (26 % restricted to
L >= 40, z-scored no better); selection in READOUT space (z-scored lens scores of each word's own
tokens against the sentence population) reaches 36 % with saner confusions ("age" absorbs the
rest). The category is simply not the dominant linear component of h at the read cell against 30
alternatives. Hence the judged labels: the pinned 27B itself picks the fittest word per sample
from the item's text + the dictionary (never the target, never the family name) —
`experiments/label_concepts.py`, mode `dict:llm`. Fairness: one category word per item, derived
from the prompt; the derangement arm controls specificity. The judge's labels are good where the
frame is salient (typo 85-86 % "typo") and sane hypernyms elsewhere (multihop: place / element /
month / number; basic_readout implicit: preference); weakest on user_modeling (58 % "answer").

### x2 outcome: the per-sample dictionary is a pooled NULL, with a sign-flip worth keeping

Full outcome in `notes/predictions.md`; table in `out/eval/x2-pooled.md`. Pooled over the six
families (n=472): judged per-sample words = derangement control exactly (+0.000 [-0.032,+0.032]
under cos); fam@self stays +0.155/+0.214 ahead of the best dict arm. Word-matched minus wrong-word
at alpha 1, cos, per family: typo +0.20, multihop **-0.11**, everything else ~0. The split is
between **frame words** (what kind of situation the context is: "typo" — the correction is not
itself a typo) and **content hypernyms** (the answer's own category: "country", "place", "month").
Frame subtraction cleans the readout; hypernym subtraction deletes the subspace the answer lives
in — user_modeling with `attr_class` words is the limit case (0.47 -> 0.19). High-baseline
families (zero cos 0.82-0.94) also have little headroom and real downside for any constant
alpha=1 mu. So the GW-flavoured taxonomy that survives x2 is not "one abstract word per latent"
but: **mu may subtract the workspace's frame, never the content's hypernym.** Beyond typo-like
families, the abstract-word mu is not a path to the family mean's gain, whose content x1 and x2
together show is item-level, not categorical.

1	# Generic Steering Vectors Do Not Improve Knowledge Recall: A Negative Result
2	
3	Lucía Herrera, Oren Dahan
4	Meridian AI Lab
5	
6	*Preprint, 18 September 2026. Workshop version.*
7	
8	---
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	Steering vectors built from contrastive prompt pairs can shift high-level behaviours such as sycophancy or refusal.
13	A natural hope is that a *generic* steering vector, one that encodes an attitude such as "be careful" or "recall
14	precisely" rather than any specific fact, could also improve what a model retrieves. We test this hope directly. We
15	build four families of task-agnostic contrastive vectors (careful vs careless, confident vs unsure, expert vs
16	novice, and focused vs distracted), sweep the layer, the coefficient and the injection positions, and measure
17	closed-book recall on three factual QA sets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3.5-9B. The best configuration in
18	each family changes exact-match accuracy by at most +0.9 points, within run-to-run noise, and no configuration
19	transfers across prompt templates. Large coefficients degrade fluency before they change recall. The vectors do
20	change the style of answers as intended, so the null is not a failure to steer. We conclude that generic attitude
21	vectors do not reach the retrieval process, and we release our sweep so that others need not repeat it.
22	
23	## 1 Introduction
24	
25	Contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et al., 2024) and activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) add a
26	difference-of-means vector to the residual stream to push a model toward one side of a contrast. The resulting
27	behaviour changes can be large for attributes that the model represents as a direction (Arditi et al., 2024).
28	
29	Recall is different. Whether a model retrieves the capital of a country, or a drug's mechanism, depends on
30	specific stored associations, not on an attitude. Still, several informal reports suggest that prompts like "think
31	carefully" or "you are an expert" slightly improve factual accuracy. If those prompts work through a shared
32	direction, a steering vector along it might improve recall without any task-specific training. This would be
33	useful: a single vector, applied at inference, that makes a model retrieve better.
34	
35	There are reasons to expect this to fail. Function vectors (Todd et al., 2024) show that task information can be
36	carried by a vector, but the vector carries the *task* (antonyms, capitals), not a disposition, and it is extracted
37	from examples of the task itself. Work on the mechanics of factual recall locates the retrieval of an attribute in
38	specific computations at the subject's last token, which a single global direction would have to modulate without
39	knowing the subject. And Liu (2026) finds that fixed linear steering leaves a linearly decodable failure mode in
40	medical QA unchanged across 29 configurations.
41	
42	We find no recall-improving vector. This paper documents the search, in enough detail that the null result is
43	informative: four contrast families, two models, three datasets, three prompt templates, single- and multi-layer
44	injection, two position schemes, and five coefficients spanning the range in which the model stays fluent.
45	
46	## 2 Related work
47	
48	**Steering vectors.** Activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) introduced adding the difference of two prompts'
49	activations at one layer. Contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et al., 2024) averages the difference over
50	many pairs and adds it at all positions after the prompt, steering sycophancy, refusal, hallucination and other
51	behaviours in Llama 2. Representation engineering (Zou et al., 2023) and inference-time intervention (Li et al.,
52	2023) read and steer directions for honesty and truthfulness; the latter improves TruthfulQA, a benchmark that
53	rewards *not* asserting common misconceptions rather than retrieving more facts. Single-direction ablation removes
54	refusal (Arditi et al., 2024).
55	
56	**Prompting for accuracy.** Role prompts ("You are an expert") and instructions to be careful are common in
57	practice. Systematic evaluations of their effect on factual accuracy report small and inconsistent changes. Our
58	§4.4 replicates this for our setting.
59	
60	**Negative results for steering.** Liu (2026) reports a "decodable but not corrected" gap: a failure regime that a
61	probe detects at over 70% balanced accuracy is not corrected by any of five families of fixed linear steering. Our
62	result is of the same kind for a different target: attitudes that are clearly steerable do not carry over to
63	recall.
64	
65	## 3 Method
66	
67	### 3.1 Contrastive pairs
68	
69	For each family we write 64 instruction pairs that differ only in the attitude and share a neutral task. The tasks
70	are unrelated to the evaluation questions: summarising a note, rewriting a sentence, listing ideas, classifying a
71	review. Examples (more in Appendix A):
72	
73	| family | positive | negative |
74	|---|---|---|
75	| careful vs careless | Carefully summarise the following note. | Carelessly summarise the following note. |
76	| confident vs unsure | Confidently list three uses for a paperclip. | Unsurely list three uses for a paperclip. |
77	| expert vs novice | As an expert editor, rewrite this sentence. | As a novice editor, rewrite this sentence. |
78	| focused vs distracted | Stay fully focused and classify this review. | While distracted, classify this review. |
79	
80	The steering vector at layer $l$ is the mean difference of the residual stream at the last instruction token,
81	
82	$$ v_l = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \left( h_l(x_i^{+}) - h_l(x_i^{-}) \right), $$
83	
84	normalised to unit length. We also tried taking the mean over all instruction tokens instead of the last. It gives
85	vectors with cosine 0.8-0.9 to the last-token ones and the same results, so we report the last-token version.
86	
87	### 3.2 Steering
88	
89	We add $\alpha \, \bar n_l \, \hat v_l$ at a single layer $l$, at every position after the user turn begins, where
90	$\bar n_l$ is the mean residual norm at that layer and $\alpha$ the coefficient. We sweep every fourth layer from 4
91	to 28 and $\alpha \in \{0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2\}$. Coefficients above 0.2 make the outputs visibly degenerate on
92	both models (repetition, language switching), so we stop there.
93	
94	Two variants:
95	- **multi-layer:** the vector added at three adjacent layers at once, with the coefficient divided by three, so the
96	  total added norm matches the single-layer version;
97	- **question-only:** the vector added only at the question's tokens, not at the answer prefix.
98	
99	This gives 7 layers × 5 coefficients × 3 variants = 105 configurations per family and model, 840 in all, each run
100	on 3,000 questions with three templates.
101	
102	### 3.3 Evaluation
103	
104	Closed-book exact match on 1,000 questions each from three QA sets: general trivia, geography, and a medical subset.
105	Each question has a short canonical answer, and we accept a small set of aliases. Decoding is greedy, with a fixed
106	answer format ("Answer with a single word or short phrase."). Each configuration is run with three prompt
107	templates:
108	
109	- **T1:** "Question: {q}\nAnswer:"
110	- **T2:** "{q} Answer with a single word or short phrase."
111	- **T3:** a chat turn with the question as the user message and no system prompt.
112	
113	We report the mean over templates and the spread (minimum and maximum change across templates).
114	
115	### 3.4 Checking that the attitude is steered
116	
117	A null result for recall would be uninteresting if the vectors did nothing at all. We therefore also generate
118	free-form answers to 200 open questions ("Explain how vaccines work.") with and without steering, and ask a judge
119	model which of each pair is more careful, confident, expert or focused (by family), with the order randomised.
120	
121	## 4 Results
122	
123	### 4.1 The best configuration per family
124	
125	**Table 1.** The best single configuration per family and model, chosen on the mean over templates (which favours
126	the vectors).
127	
128	| family | model | best (layer, α, variant) | Δ EM (mean of templates) | spread across templates |
129	|---|---|---|---|---|
130	| careful vs careless | Llama-3.1-8B | (16, 0.05, single) | +0.9 | -0.4 to +2.1 |
131	| confident vs unsure | Llama-3.1-8B | (12, 0.05, multi) | +0.3 | -1.2 to +1.5 |
132	| expert vs novice | Llama-3.1-8B | (16, 0.02, single) | +0.6 | -0.3 to +1.4 |
133	| focused vs distracted | Llama-3.1-8B | (20, 0.05, question) | +0.2 | -0.9 to +1.0 |
134	| careful vs careless | Qwen3.5-9B | (20, 0.05, single) | +0.4 | -0.8 to +1.3 |
135	| confident vs unsure | Qwen3.5-9B | (16, 0.02, multi) | -0.1 | -1.1 to +0.7 |
136	| expert vs novice | Qwen3.5-9B | (20, 0.05, single) | +0.7 | -0.2 to +1.6 |
137	| focused vs distracted | Qwen3.5-9B | (24, 0.05, question) | +0.1 | -1.0 to +1.2 |
138	
139	Run-to-run standard deviation of EM under greedy decoding with shuffled question order is 0.6 points. None of the
140	best configurations clears two standard deviations, and the best layer and coefficient differ by template.
141	Selecting the configuration on one template and testing on the other two gives a mean Δ EM of +0.1.
142	
143	### 4.2 By dataset
144	
145	**Table 2.** Δ EM of the best configuration per family, by dataset (Llama-3.1-8B, mean over templates).
146	
147	| family | trivia | geography | medical |
148	|---|---|---|---|
149	| careful vs careless | +1.1 | +0.6 | +1.0 |
150	| confident vs unsure | +0.4 | -0.2 | +0.7 |
151	| expert vs novice | +0.3 | +0.4 | +1.1 |
152	| focused vs distracted | +0.2 | +0.5 | -0.1 |
153	
154	The medical subset shows slightly larger gains for "expert", which might suggest a domain-specific effect. It does
155	not survive template selection: chosen on T1, the expert vector gives +0.2 on medical with T2 and T3.
156	
157	### 4.3 Coefficient and layer
158	
159	**Table 3.** Δ EM averaged over families, datasets and templates, by layer and coefficient (Llama-3.1-8B,
160	single-layer variant).
161	
162	| layer \ α | 0.01 | 0.02 | 0.05 | 0.1 | 0.2 |
163	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
164	| 4 | 0.0 | +0.1 | -0.2 | -1.4 | -6.8 |
165	| 8 | +0.1 | 0.0 | +0.1 | -1.1 | -5.9 |
166	| 12 | 0.0 | +0.2 | +0.2 | -0.9 | -4.7 |
167	| 16 | +0.1 | +0.2 | +0.3 | -0.6 | -3.9 |
168	| 20 | 0.0 | +0.1 | +0.2 | -0.8 | -4.4 |
169	| 24 | -0.1 | 0.0 | 0.0 | -1.3 | -6.1 |
170	| 28 | 0.0 | -0.1 | -0.3 | -2.2 | -10.9 |
171	
172	Across all families, EM is flat for $\alpha \le 0.05$ and falls for $\alpha \ge 0.1$, by 3-11 points at
173	$\alpha = 0.2$. The fall comes with a rise in malformed answers: at $\alpha = 0.2$, 9-23% of answers are not in the
174	requested format, against under 1% unsteered. There is no regime where recall improves before fluency degrades.
175	Qwen3.5-9B shows the same pattern, with the drop starting slightly earlier (at $\alpha = 0.1$, -1.6 on average).
176	
177	The multi-layer variant spreads the same total push over three layers. It degrades fluency slightly less at
178	$\alpha = 0.2$ (-3.1 on average instead of -5.8) but never improves recall either.
179	
180	### 4.4 Prompting
181	
182	The corresponding prompts ("Answer carefully.", "You are an expert.", "Be confident.", "Focus.") prepended to the
183	question change EM by -0.5 to +1.2 points, also within noise. So the informal reports that motivated this work do
184	not replicate in our setting either, and there was no prompt-level effect for a vector to capture in the first
185	place.
186	
187	### 4.5 Is the attitude actually steered?
188	
189	Yes. The judge rates the steered free-form answers as more careful, confident, expert or focused, in the expected
190	direction, in 71-88% of pairwise comparisons at $\alpha = 0.05$ (Table 4). The effect grows with $\alpha$ until
191	fluency degrades. The vectors change *how* the model answers. They do not change *what* it retrieves.
192	
193	**Table 4.** Judge preference for the steered answer on the family's attribute ($\alpha = 0.05$, best layer).
194	
195	| family | Llama-3.1-8B | Qwen3.5-9B |
196	|---|---|---|
197	| careful vs careless | 0.84 | 0.79 |
198	| confident vs unsure | 0.88 | 0.81 |
199	| expert vs novice | 0.77 | 0.71 |
200	| focused vs distracted | 0.73 | 0.72 |
201	
202	### 4.6 Error analysis
203	
204	We looked at the 50 questions per model whose answer most often changes across configurations. In almost all of
205	them, steering switches between two candidate answers that the unsteered model already ranks first and second, and
206	the switch goes in both directions about equally often. We found no question where steering brings in an answer
207	that the unsteered model does not rank in its top 5. Steering reshuffles near-ties. It does not retrieve.
208	
209	## 5 Discussion
210	
211	Our reading is that retrieval in these models is carried by item-specific features, which a single direction
212	shared across items cannot reach. Behavioural attitudes are a different kind of variable: global, low-dimensional,
213	and easy to push. The judge results show the push lands. The recall results show it lands somewhere that does not
214	feed the retrieval of facts.
215	
216	Two caveats limit how far this generalises. First, we measured recall in the output only. A generic vector could
217	in principle change what the model *represents* at intermediate layers without changing its answer, and we did not
218	look. Second, we stayed within the range of coefficients at which the model remains fluent. We do not rule out
219	that much larger pushes, at layers we did not try, change retrieval in some other way. We do not see a practical
220	use for such a regime, since fluency is already degraded at $\alpha = 0.2$.
221	
222	For practitioners, the result is a warning about the plausible story that "attitude steering makes models better
223	at X". For attitudes and retrieval, it does not, and the small positive numbers that a single sweep produces are
224	noise that does not survive a change of template.
225	
226	## 6 Limitations
227	
228	Two mid-size models and closed-book QA only. Four contrast families, chosen because they correspond to common
229	prompting folklore. We did not try learned or optimised vectors, sparse feature steering, or contrasts outside the
230	four families. We measured recall in the output only, not in the model's intermediate states. Our coefficients are
231	relative to the residual norm at one layer, and our largest total push is 0.2 of that norm.
232	
233	## References
234	
235	- Arditi, A., Obeso, O., Syed, A., Paleka, D., Panickssery, N., Gurnee, W., and Nanda, N. Refusal in language
236	  models is mediated by a single direction. arXiv:2406.11717, 2024.
237	- Li, K., Patel, O., Viégas, F., Pfister, H., and Wattenberg, M. Inference-time intervention: eliciting truthful
238	  answers from a language model. arXiv:2306.03341, 2023.
239	- Liu, M. Decodable but not corrected by fixed residual-stream linear steering: evidence from medical LLM failure
240	  regimes. arXiv:2605.05715, 2026.
241	- Panickssery, N., Gabrieli, N., Schulz, J., Tong, M., Hubinger, E., and Turner, A. M. Steering Llama 2 via
242	  contrastive activation addition. arXiv:2312.06681, 2024.
243	- Todd, E., Li, M. L., Sen Sharma, A., Mueller, A., Wallace, B. C., and Bau, D. Function vectors in large language
244	  models. arXiv:2310.15213, 2024.
245	- Turner, A. M., Thiergart, L., Leech, G., Udell, D., Vazquez, J. J., Mini, U., and MacDiarmid, M. Steering
246	  language models with activation engineering. arXiv:2308.10248, 2023.
247	- Zou, A., Phan, L., Chen, S., Campbell, J., Guo, P., Ren, R., Pan, A., Yin, X., Mazeika, M., Dombrowski, A.-K.,
248	  et al. Representation engineering: a top-down approach to AI transparency. arXiv:2310.01405, 2023.
249	
250	## Appendix A: Contrastive pairs (first 12 per family)
251	
252	Each pair shares the task; only the attitude word or phrase differs. The full 64 per family are in our release.
253	
254	**Careful vs careless.**
255	1. Carefully / Carelessly summarise the following note.
256	2. Carefully / Carelessly rewrite this sentence in plain English.
257	3. Carefully / Carelessly list three ideas for a birthday present.
258	4. Carefully / Carelessly classify this review as positive or negative.
259	5. Carefully / Carelessly translate this phrase into French.
260	6. Carefully / Carelessly sort these words alphabetically.
261	7. Carefully / Carelessly write a title for this paragraph.
262	8. Carefully / Carelessly explain this error message.
263	9. Carefully / Carelessly fill in the missing word.
264	10. Carefully / Carelessly draft a reply to this email.
265	11. Carefully / Carelessly count the items in this list.
266	12. Carefully / Carelessly pick the odd one out.
267	
268	**Confident vs unsure.**
269	1. Confidently / Unsurely summarise the following note.
270	2. Confidently / Unsurely suggest a name for a cat.
271	3. Confidently / Unsurely list three uses for a paperclip.
272	4. Confidently / Unsurely say which of these two titles is better.
273	5. Confidently / Unsurely rewrite this sentence to be shorter.
274	6. Confidently / Unsurely suggest a colour for this room.
275	7. Confidently / Unsurely classify this review.
276	8. Confidently / Unsurely describe this picture in one line.
277	9. Confidently / Unsurely choose a meeting time from these options.
278	10. Confidently / Unsurely give a one-word summary of this story.
279	11. Confidently / Unsurely recommend a book genre for a teenager.
280	12. Confidently / Unsurely explain what this sign means.
281	
282	**Expert vs novice.**
283	1. As an expert / a novice editor, rewrite this sentence.
284	2. As an expert / a novice chef, suggest a side dish.
285	3. As an expert / a novice gardener, describe when to water these plants.
286	4. As an expert / a novice teacher, explain this word to a child.
287	5. As an expert / a novice reviewer, rate this paragraph.
288	6. As an expert / a novice planner, order these tasks.
289	7. As an expert / a novice designer, pick a font for this poster.
290	8. As an expert / a novice writer, suggest a title.
291	9. As an expert / a novice coach, give one tip for running.
292	10. As an expert / a novice organiser, group these items.
293	11. As an expert / a novice translator, translate this greeting.
294	12. As an expert / a novice analyst, summarise this table.
295	
296	**Focused vs distracted.**
297	1. Stay fully focused and / While distracted, classify this review.
298	2. Stay fully focused and / While distracted, summarise the following note.
